en.title: Tickets and timetables
en.summary: Buying tickets, reading a timetable and choosing the best journey.

paragraphs: A timetable gives you times in a compact format, and a ticket office asks you for dates and a choice of fares. In this lesson you will read and ask about both.
A customer is buying a train ticket at Reading station.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Yes. What time is the next train?

lines.speaker: Clerk
lines.text: At 14:30, from platform six. There are also trains at 15:00 and 15:30.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: And when is the last one back?

lines.speaker: Clerk
lines.text: The last one leaves Oxford at 23:00.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Is there a cheaper ticket for travelling after ten?

lines.speaker: Clerk
lines.text: Yes, an off-peak return is cheaper. It is valid after nine thirty.

paragraphs: **1. The 24-hour clock appears on timetables.** Say thirteen hundred or one o'clock; in speech people usually use the 12-hour clock with half past, quarter to and so on. See Introduction to Grammar: Numerals.

blocks.html:
TimetableSpoken
14:30half past two
15:45quarter to four
23:00eleven o'clock at night
09:10ten past nine

paragraphs: **2. Next, last and first are ordinal adjectives.** They go before the noun and tell the position in a series. See Introduction to Grammar: Adjectives.

blocks.html:
WordExample
nextthe next train
lastthe last bus
firstthe first flight in the morning
secondthe second platform on the left

items: Off-peak tickets are cheaper because they avoid the busy times.
Valid means that a ticket can be used; expired means it can no longer be used.
A season ticket allows unlimited travel for a week, a month or a year.
Check the departure board for platform changes.

paragraphs: In Britain buying a ticket online in advance can be much cheaper than buying one on the day. Many people use a railcard, which gives about a third off most fares.
